questions.q: Why should an API key or password never be placed directly into a prompt or system prompt?
options: A context window can be logged, traced, summarized into memory, or read back out through prompt injection, so a secret placed there should be treated as already leaked
Prompts are always encrypted automatically by every LLM provider
Placing secrets in a prompt is fine as long as the application has no internet access
Models are physically incapable of repeating any text from their own context window
questions.explain: A context window isn't a private scratchpad — it can surface through logging, observability traces, memory summarization, or an attacker-induced repetition via prompt injection, so a secret placed there counts as exposed.

questions.q: What is the core architectural fix this lesson describes for keeping credentials away from a model's reasoning?
options: Encrypting the prompt text so the model cannot read its own instructions
Giving the model a separate, lower-privilege copy of every credential it might need
Separating the reasoning plane from the credential plane, so the model only supplies intent and parameters while the orchestration layer injects real credentials at tool-execution time
Removing all tools from the agent so it never needs any credentials
questions.explain: The model decides that a tool should be called and with what arguments, but never holds or sees the credential — the orchestration layer around it holds and injects real credentials only at the moment a tool actually executes.

questions.q: What does managed identity / workload identity federation (from Course 9's cloud security content) provide for an AI application's service-to-service calls?
options: A way to encrypt long-lived API keys so they are safe to store in a prompt
A faster way to generate static API keys for every tool an agent uses
A requirement that every tool call be approved by a human before it runs
Authentication based on an identity tied to the compute resource itself, with short-lived tokens issued automatically — removing the need for a stored long-lived key entirely
questions.explain: Managed identity ties authentication to the compute resource rather than a stored secret, so there's no long-lived key to leak through a log, config file, or container image — the token is short-lived and automatically rotated.

questions.q: When does a dedicated secrets vault (such as Key Vault, Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault) still earn its place in an AI application, even after adopting managed identity broadly?
options: Never — managed identity always eliminates every secret an AI application could need
Only for secrets used during model training, never for production credentials
For the remaining credentials that managed identity can't replace, such as a third-party API that only accepts a static key or a legacy system with no identity federation support
Only when the application has no tool-calling capability at all
questions.explain: Managed identity doesn't eliminate every secret — some third-party or legacy systems still require a static key. For those, a vault provides encryption at rest, auditable access, and rotation without a code change.

questions.q: Why should training, fine-tuning, and RAG-indexing data be scanned for accidentally embedded secrets before use?
options: Because scanning data for secrets is required only by RAG pipelines, never by fine-tuning pipelines
Because a credential baked into training data or an indexed document can resurface later through ordinary model output, the same way other memorized training data can leak back out
Because training data is never stored anywhere after a model finishes training
Because fine-tuning pipelines automatically redact any sensitive data without configuration
questions.explain: A secret embedded in data used to train, fine-tune, or populate an index becomes part of what the model can memorize and later reproduce through normal use — the same training-data-leakage risk covered earlier in the course, applied to credentials specifically.
